name: Pakistan

facts.religion: Sunni Islam about 85%, Shia about 12%, Christian and Hindu minorities

system_note: The army is the dominant power behind the civilian government.
snapshot: Pakistan brokered the US-Iran ceasefire and hosted the first direct talks in decades, while fighting its own war against the Taliban next door.
culture: Pakistan's culture draws on Punjabi, Sindhi, Pashtun, Baloch and Mohajir traditions, with Urdu as the common language. Qawwali, the Sufi devotional music made famous by Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan, and Sufi shrines are central to popular Islam. Cricket is a national obsession; Imran Khan led the team to the 1992 World Cup. Truck art is a famous folk style.
society: The army has ruled directly for decades at a time and shapes politics behind the scenes. The economy has survived repeated balance of payments crises with IMF help. Floods in 2022 submerged a third of the country. Insurgencies in Balochistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa claim many lives each year.
situation: For most of the past 20 years, Washington saw Pakistan as a problem: an unreliable ally that sheltered the Taliban and hid Osama bin Laden. In 2026, it became the country America relied on to talk to Iran.

When the US and Israel attacked Iran on 28 February, Pakistan, which borders Iran and has ties to both sides, moved quickly. It brokered the 8 April ceasefire, and on 11 and 12 April hosted the first face-to-face US-Iranian talks in decades in Islamabad, with Vice President JD Vance leading the American side (Atlantic Council). The man behind it was Field Marshal Asim Munir, the army chief, who built a close relationship with Trump after the brief India-Pakistan war in May 2025 and flew repeatedly to Tehran. Iran's ambassador said Tehran would "do talks in Pakistan and nowhere else, because we trust Pakistan" (Washington Times). The White House called Pakistan the "only mediator." Yet on its other border, Pakistan was fighting its own war: from February it carried out airstrikes in Afghanistan and declared "open war" on the Taliban government over militants attacking Pakistani soldiers. At home, power has shifted decisively to the army, with Munir's elevation to chief of defence forces, while former prime minister Imran Khan, the country's most popular politician, remains in prison.
power: Formally a federal parliamentary republic, with a prime minister accountable to the National Assembly. In practice the army has ruled directly for decades at a time and remains the dominant power, shaping foreign and security policy and deciding which civilian governments survive.
holders: Field Marshal Asim Munir, Chief of Defence Forces; Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif.
